The security instrument concerns an interest supporting an obligation and its treatment in the property records. It does not rewrite the note, prove project profitability, or eliminate senior liens. Recording and negotiability therefore answer different questions. A recorded instrument can secure a risky obligation, and the existence of collateral does not establish compliance with a separate securities requirement.

1093.title: A secured promise with a profits condition: Treat nonnegotiability as absence of every obligation
1093.lessonTitle: Purchase agreements, options, leases, and notes
1093.text: Failure of a negotiability requirement does not automatically make the entire contractual arrangement void. Negotiability is a specialized classification with specific requirements. Ordinary contract enforceability asks other questions about assent, consideration, lawful purpose, capacity, and terms. A condition may prevent negotiability while leaving an enforceable conditional promise. Whether this particular agreement or offering is enforceable still requires full analysis; the classification alone cannot resolve every other defect or regulatory issue.

1094.title: A power to buy is not the same as first refusal
1094.lessonTitle: Purchase agreements, options, leases, and notes
1094.text: A power to buy is not the same as first refusal A lease-option combines separate possession and purchase rights. Paying rent alone does not necessarily exercise the option or create purchase equity. Option The holder can elect to purchase on agreed terms within the option period. Exercise must comply with the option; the holder is not initially required to buy. Right of first refusal A specified event triggers an opportunity to purchase under the agreement. The holder cannot necessarily force the owner to offer a sale now.

1095.title: Follow the interest the original tenant retains
1095.lessonTitle: Purchase agreements, options, leases, and notes
1095.text: Follow the interest the original tenant retains Check consent requirements and the actual interest transferred. Neither structure automatically releases the original tenant from the lease obligations owed to the landlord. Assignment Transfers the remaining leasehold interest in the typical case. Example: all three remaining years pass to the replacement occupant. Sublease Transfers a lesser interest while the original tenant retains a reversionary interest. Example: two of three remaining years pass, with the final year retained.

1096.title: A price amendment need not increase the loan
1096.lessonTitle: Purchase agreements, options, leases, and notes
1096.text: A price amendment need not increase the loan Stipulated amendment and lender commitment; no other charges, impounds, or prorations. The paid deposit is credited once, and the seller cost credit does not reduce the stated $660,000 price. Amended price: original $640,000 plus $20,000 660000 Unchanged new-loan proceeds -496000 Deposit already paid -16000 Buyer closing costs 12000 Permitted seller credit toward costs -5000 Additional cash due 155000 The original calculation was $135,000. With everything else fixed, the $20,000 price increase raises additional cash by the same $20,000. Recalculate additional buyer cash after a signed price increase while the loan, paid deposit, costs, and credit remain fixed.

1097.title: Early possession can change the casualty-risk result
1097.lessonTitle: Purchase agreements, options, leases, and notes
1097.text: Early possession can change the casualty-risk result This is a default-rule comparison, not an insurance coverage determination. Fault, nonmaterial damage before transfer, and negotiated risk clauses can change the problem. Assume the purchase contract does not expressly change section 1662, an accidental fire materially destroys the property, neither party is at fault, and no other issue affects the result. The fire cases below are alternatives. The statutory switch is title OR possession, subject to its conditions and an express contrary agreement. Moving in early can change the analysis before closing. Alternative A: fire before title or possession Before either transfer Neither legal title nor possession has passed. The seller cannot enforce the contract under section 1662(a), and the buyer can recover price payments. Buyer receives possession Early occupancy In the alternative sequence, the buyer takes possession before the deed transfer. This is a legally consequential event, not just a scheduling convenience. Alternative B: fire after early occupancy After possession; before title Possession has passed even though title has not. Under section 1662(b), that casualty alone does not relieve the buyer of paying or entitle recovery of price already paid. Apply Civil Code 1662 before and after possession transfers, without treating recordation as the only trigger.

1098.title: Timely notice may satisfy only half the exercise clause
1098.lessonTitle: Purchase agreements, options, leases, and notes
1098.text: Timely notice may satisfy only half the exercise clause No universal payment deadline is asserted. This illustration tests the clear terms actually given, not every equitable issue in an option dispute. Purchase option / Exercise conditions Original educational excerpt, not for execution. Assume a valid supported option, clear conditions, and no waiver or other exception. Read what constitutes exercise separately from what happens after exercise. A different option requiring notice alone would create a different case. Underlying bargain $525,000 purchase price The holder may exercise this bargain, not unilaterally substitute a lower price or new contingency. Required notice Unconditional written exercise received by 4 p.m. on August 20 The contract requires receipt, not merely sending the notice before the deadline. Required exercise payment $5,000 received with exercise by that deadline This payment is an express exercise condition, not merely an amount due at a later closing. Actual performance Notice received at 3 p.m.; payment first tendered the next day Timely notice alone does not satisfy both of the stipulated exercise conditions. Distinguish notice, exercise payment, and later closing performance in a stipulated purchase option.

1099.title: Rent paid and potential purchase credit do not grow together
1099.lessonTitle: Purchase agreements, options, leases, and notes
1099.text: Rent paid and potential purchase credit do not grow together Fictional terms: $2,000 monthly rent; $400 credit only for timely payments; month 4 is paid late and earns no credit, without otherwise ending the option. The $3,000 option fee is separately paid and credited at closing. Lines connect month-end observations, not daily accrual or present ownership equity. Completed rental month Cumulative amount After six months the tenant has paid $12,000 rent plus $3,000 option consideration. The potential credit is only $3,000 + five qualifying $400 credits = $5,000, contingent on proper exercise and closing. Rent actually paid 0 0 1 2000 2 4000 3 6000 4 8000 5 10000 6 12000 Potential closing credit 0 3000 1 3400 2 3800 3 4200 4 4200 5 4600 6 5000 Trace a lease-option credit that accrues only for qualifying payments and distinguish it from rent paid or ownership equity.

1100.title: A first-refusal right starts with the agreed trigger
1100.lessonTitle: Purchase agreements, options, leases, and notes
1100.text: A first-refusal right starts with the agreed trigger The five-day period and trigger are invented contractual terms, not California-wide defaults. Package sales, transfers to affiliates, gifts, and altered third-party terms require reading the actual agreement and law. A valid fictional right applies when the owner decides to accept a bona fide third-party purchase offer; it requires notice of those terms and allows five calendar days after receipt to match. What follows? Owner declines every offer The holder wants to force a sale today for $400,000, but the agreement sets no such fixed-price purchase power. The stated first-refusal trigger has not occurred. Do not turn it into an option the owner never granted. Owner decides to accept $450,000 cash The notice communicates the qualifying offer and the agreed response period begins on receipt. The holder must follow the matching procedure and applicable terms, not rely on an old informal price discussion. Holder requests $440,000 and financing The response changes both price and financing instead of matching the noticed cash offer. The proposed new bargain is not a match under the stipulated right merely because it arrives within five days. Apply a specific first-refusal trigger and matching process instead of treating the right as an immediately exercisable fixed-price option.

1101.title: The retained final year identifies the lesser interest
1101.lessonTitle: Purchase agreements, options, leases, and notes
1101.text: The retained final year identifies the lesser interest Classification follows the interest transferred, not the document's heading. Residential protective statutes and any actual renewal or default would require separate treatment. A tenant has all of 2027-2029 remaining on a valid commercial lease. Required consent is obtained; no release, extension, or holdover occurs. Change the grant to the entire remaining 2027-2029 term and the classification moves toward assignment, but release from promised rent still requires a separate basis. Subtenant takes the entire premises January 1, 2027 The original tenant grants possession only through December 31, 2028 and retains the last year of the head lease. The granted term ends December 31, 2028 The subtenant's stated two-year interest ends, while the original tenant still has a year of leasehold rights. Original tenant retains the final year During 2029 That retained reversionary interval explains why this is a sublease rather than an assignment of the entire remaining term. Head lease reaches its stated end December 31, 2029 The original tenant's contractual responsibility was not erased merely by granting the sublease. Use actual term boundaries to identify a sublease and distinguish possession ending from release of the original tenant's promises.

1102.title: Fixed principal and variable interest can coexist
1102.lessonTitle: Purchase agreements, options, leases, and notes
1102.text: Fixed principal and variable interest can coexist Negotiability is not a credit rating, guarantee of payment, or proof that selling an investment is exempt from securities law. Promissory note / Selected teaching terms Original educational excerpt, not for execution. Assume a signed unconditional promise and all other negotiability requirements; no prohibited additional undertaking is included. Test each requirement. Neither a variable rate nor a permitted security reference automatically makes this otherwise qualifying promise nonnegotiable. Principal and payee $100,000 payable to the order of Example Lender Identify the fixed money principal and the designated recipient; this is not a deed conveying the property. Maturity December 1, 2027 The stipulated date makes payment timing definite rather than dependent on an unspecified successful project. Interest description Published index plus the stated margin, reset as specified Section 3112 permits variable rates and references to outside information; variability alone is not a negotiability defect. Collateral reference See the identified deed of trust for collateral rights A permitted reference concerning security is distinct from making the payment promise subject to another agreement. Read a note's principal, payee, maturity, variable-interest term, and security reference without automatically disqualifying negotiability.

1103.title: A payment condition differs from a limited payment source
1103.lessonTitle: Purchase agreements, options, leases, and notes
1103.text: A payment condition differs from a limited payment source Read the operative words, not only whether an outside document or project is mentioned. Source limitation and event-conditioned liability require different analysis. Express condition The maker owes payment only if a specified project obtains approval. The promise expressly conditions payment on an outside event. That raises an unconditional-promise defect; a contract may still exist even if the writing is not negotiable. Limited source The promise is payable from an identified fund only, with no other express condition. Section 3106(b)(2) says a particular-fund or source limitation does not itself make the promise conditional. Check all other negotiability requirements; do not infer a repayment guarantee from this narrow rule. Collateral reference The note refers to a deed of trust for collateral, prepayment, or acceleration rights. Section 3106(b)(1) permits those references without making the promise conditional for that reason. This differs from saying all payment rights are subject to a separate agreement. Apply Commercial Code 3106 to express conditions, collateral references, and limited-source language without treating them as equivalent.

1104.title: The same seller-financed balance can use different title arrangements
1104.lessonTitle: Purchase agreements, options, leases, and notes
1104.text: The same seller-financed balance can use different title arrangements Assume valid instruments and no other liens or financing. Equal payment arithmetic does not establish equal title interests, remedies, or recording consequences. Installment land sale contract Price is $400,000; buyer pays $100,000 and owes $300,000 under the stipulated five-year installment terms. Seller retains legal title until the agreed five-year payment obligation is completed; buyer generally acquires an equitable interest. Do not infer an automatic forfeiture of all payments after default; remedies and protective rules require separate analysis. Deed delivered; seller takes security The same $100,000 cash and $300,000 financing fund a completed conveyance to the buyer. The $300,000 note states the debt; a deed of trust secures it for the seller as beneficiary. The seller is a secured creditor, not an owner simply retaining the entire fee until every payment is made. Distinguish retained legal title under an installment land contract from a completed conveyance secured by a seller-held deed of trust.
